n:
*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term מַשָּׂא (massaʾ, “pronouncement”) is derived from the root נָשָׂא (nasaʾ, “to lift”) and probably connected to the phrase “to raise one’s voice” (HALOT 639 s.v. II מַשָּׂא), that is, the message that was raised or called out. See the note at {{Isaiah 13:1|Isa 13:1}}. The form may be absolute or construct. If absolute, the term stands alone (so NAB, NRSV), if construct it would be joined with what follows, “the burden [or “revelation”] of” (so KJV, NASB, ESV). Since the following phrase is a synonym, it is likely absolute, in apposition to “the Lord’s message.”

*Translator's note:* There is some question as to whether מַלְאָכִי (malʾakhi) should be understood as a personal name (so almost all English versions) or as simply “my messenger” (the literal meaning of the Hebrew). Despite the fact that the word should be understood in the latter sense in {{Malachi 3:1|3:1}} (where, however, it refers to a different person), to understand it that way here would result in the book being of anonymous authorship, a situation anomalous among all the prophetic literature of the OT.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and I loved Jacob, but Esau I hated.” The context indicates this is technical covenant vocabulary in which “love” and “hate” are synonymous with “choose” and “reject” respectively (see {{Deuteronomy 7:8|Deut 7:8}}; Jer 31:3; Hos 3:1; 9:15; 11:1).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his”; the referent (Esau) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I set his mountains as a desolation.”

*Translator's note:* Or “inheritance” (so NIV, NLT).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “jackals of the wilderness.”

*Study note:* *Edom*, a “brother” nation to Israel, became almost paradigmatic of hostility toward Israel and God (see {{Numbers 20:14|Num 20:14-21}}; {{Deuteronomy 2:8|Deut 2:8}}; Jer 49:7-22; {{Ezekiel 25:12|Ezek 25:12-14}}; {{Amos 1:11|Amos 1:11-12}}; {{Obadiah 10|Obad 10-12}}).

*Study note:* The epithet *Lord of Heaven’s Armies* occurs frequently as a divine title throughout Malachi (24 times total). This name (יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת, yehvah tsevaʾot), traditionally translated “Lord of hosts” (so KJV, NAB, NASB; cf. NIV NLT “Lord Almighty”; NCV, CEV “Lord All-Powerful”), emphasizes the majestic sovereignty of the Lord, an especially important concept in the postexilic world of great human empires and rulers. For a thorough study of the divine title, see T. N. D. Mettinger, *In Search of God*, 123-57.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and they will call them.” The third person plural subject is indefinite; one could translate, “and people will call them.”
*Translator's note:* Or “Great is the Lord” (so NAB; similar NIV, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* The verb “respects” is not in the Hebrew text but is supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons. It is understood by ellipsis (see “honors” in the preceding line).

*Translator's note:* The pronoun “your” is supplied in the translation for clarification (also a second time before “master” later in this verse).

*Study note:* The word *table*, here a synonym for “altar,” has overtones of covenant imagery in which a feast shared by the covenant partners was an important element (see {{Exodus 24:11|Exod 24:11}}). It also draws attention to the analogy of sitting down at a common meal with the governor (v. {{Malachi 1:8|8}}).

*Study note:* Offerings of animals that were *lame* or *sick* were strictly forbidden by the Mosaic law (see {{Deuteronomy 15:21|Deut 15:21}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “it” (so NAB, NASB). Contemporary English more naturally uses a plural pronoun to agree with “the lame and sick” in the previous question (cf. NIV, NCV).

*Text-critical note:* The LXX and Vulgate read “with it” (which in Hebrew would be הֲיִרְצֵהוּ, hayirtsehu, a reading followed by NAB) rather than “with you” of the MT (הֲיִרְצְךָ, hayirtsekha). The MT (followed here by most English versions) is to be preferred because of the parallel with the following phrase פָנֶיךָ (fanekha, “receive you,” which the present translation renders as “show you favor”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “seek the face of God.”

*Translator's note:* After the imperative, the prefixed verbal form with *vav* conjunction indicates purpose (cf. NASB, NRSV).

*Study note:* The rhetorical language suggests that as long as the priesthood and people remain disobedient, the *temple doors* may as well be closed because God is not “at home” to receive them or their worship there.

*Study note:* *My name will be great among the nations*. In what is clearly a strongly ironic shift of thought, the Lord contrasts the unbelief and virtual paganism of the postexilic community with the conversion and obedience of the nations that will one day worship the God of Israel.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “fruit.” The following word “food” in the Hebrew text (אָכְלוֹ, ʾokhlo) appears to be an explanatory gloss to clarify the meaning of the rare word נִיב (niv, “fruit”; see {{Isaiah 57:19|Isa 57:19}} *Qere*; נוֹב, nov, “fruit,” in *Kethib*). Cf. ASV “the fruit thereof, even its food.” In this cultic context the reference is to the offerings on the altar.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from your hand,” a metonymy of part (the hand) for whole (the person).
*Study note:* The epithet *great king* was used to describe the Hittite rulers on their covenant documents and so, in the covenant ideology of Malachi, is an apt description of the Lord.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and if you do not place upon [the] heart”; KJV, NAB, NRSV “lay it to heart.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the curse” (so NASB, NRSV); NLT “a terrible curse.”

*Text-critical note:* The phrase “discipline your children” is disputed. The LXX and Vulgate suppose זְרוֹעַ (zeroaʿ, “arm”) for the MT זֶרַע (zeraʿ, “seed”; hence, “children”). Then, for the MT גֹעֵר (goʿer, “rebuking”) the same versions suggest גָּרַע (garaʿ, “take away”). The resulting translation is “I am about to take away your arm” (cf. NAB “deprive you of the shoulder”). However, this reading is unlikely. It is common for a curse (v. {{Malachi 2:2|2}}) to fall on offspring (see, e.g., {{Deuteronomy 28:18|Deut 28:18}}, {{Deuteronomy 28:32|32}}, {{Deuteronomy 28:41|41}}, {{Deuteronomy 28:53|53}}, {{Deuteronomy 28:55|55}}, {{Deuteronomy 28:57|57}}), but a curse never takes the form of a broken or amputated arm. It is preferable to retain the reading of the MT here.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term פֶרֶשׁ (feresh, “offal”) refers to the entrails as ripped out in preparing a sacrificial victim (BDB 831 s.v. פֶּרֶשׁ). This graphic term has been variously translated: “dung” (KJV, RSV, NRSV, NLT, NIV11); “refuse” (NKJV, NASB); “offal” (NEB, NIV84).

*Study note:* See Zech 3:3-4 for similar coarse imagery which reflects cultic disqualification.

*Study note:* *My covenant* refers to the priestly covenant through Aaron and his grandson Phinehas (see {{Exodus 6:16|Exod 6:16-20}}; {{Numbers 25:10|Num 25:10-13}}; Jer 33:21-22). The point here is to contrast the priestly ideal with the disgraceful manner in which it was being carried out in postexilic times.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “True teaching was in his mouth”; cf. NASB, NRSV “True instruction (doctrine NAB) was in his mouth.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from his mouth” (so NAB, NASB, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* The definite article embedded within בַּתּוֹרָה (battorah) may suggest that *the* Torah is in mind and not just “ordinary” priestly instruction, though it might refer to the instruction previously mentioned (v. {{Malachi 2:7|7}}).

*Translator's note:* Or “the Levitical covenant.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the instruction” (so NASB). The Hebrew article is used here as a possessive pronoun (cf. NRSV, NLT).

*Study note:* The rhetorical question *Do we not all have one father?* by no means teaches the “universal fatherhood of God,” that is, that all people equally are children of God. The reference to the covenant in v. {{Malachi 2:10|10}} as well as to Israel and Judah (v. {{Malachi 2:11|11}}) makes it clear that the referent of “we” is God’s elect people.

*Translator's note:* Or perhaps “secularized”; cf. NIV “desecrated”; TEV, NLT “defiled”; CEV “disgraced.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “has married the daughter of a foreign god.” Marriage is used here as a metaphor to describe Judah’s idolatry, that is, her unfaithfulness to the Lord and “remarriage” to pagan gods. But spiritual intermarriage found expression in literal, physical marriage as well, as vv. {{Malachi 2:14|14-16}} indicate.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “tents,” used figuratively for the community here (cf. NCV, TEV); NLT “the nation of Israel.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “every man who does this, him who is awake and him who answers.” The idea seems to be a merism expressing totality, that is, everybody from the awakener to the awakened, thus “every last person who does this” (NLT similar); NIV “whoever he may be.”

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “every man who does this, him who is awake and him who answers.” For “answers” the LXX suggests an underlying Hebrew text of עָנָה (ʿanah, “to be humbled”), and then the whole phrase is modified slightly: “until he is humbled.” This requires also that the MT עֵר (ʿer, “awake”) be read as עֵד (ʿed, “until”; here the LXX reads ἕως, heōs). The reading of the LXX is most likely an alteration to correct what is arguably a difficult text.

*Study note:* *You cover the altar of the Lord with tears*. These tears are the false tears of hypocrisy, not genuine tears of repentance. The people weep because the Lord will not hear them, not because of their sin.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the Lord is a witness between you and [between] the wife of your youth.”

*Study note:* Though there is no explicit reference to marriage vows in the OT (but see {{Job 7:13|Job 7:13}}; {{Proverbs 2:17|Prov 2:17}}; {{Ezekiel 16:8|Ezek 16:8}}), the term *law* (*Heb* “covenant”) here asserts that such vows or agreements must have existed. References to divorce documents (e.g., {{Deuteronomy 24:1|Deut 24:1-3}}; Jer 3:8) also presuppose the existence of marriage documents.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and not one has done, and a remnant of the spirit to him.” The very elliptical nature of the statement suggests it is proverbial. The present translation represents an attempt to clarify the meaning of the statement (cf. NASB).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the one.” This is an oblique reference to Abraham who sought to obtain God’s blessing by circumventing God’s own plan for him by taking Hagar as wife ({{Genesis 16:1|Gen 16:1-6}}). The result of this kind of intermarriage was, of course, disastrous ({{Genesis 16:11|Gen 16:11-12}}).

*Study note:* *The wife he took in his youth* probably refers to the first wife one married (cf. NCV “the wife you married when you were young”).

*Study note:* Though the statement “I hate divorce” may (and should) be understood as a comprehensive biblical principle, the immediate context suggests that the divorce in view is that of one Jewish person by another in order to undertake subsequent marriages. The injunction here by no means contradicts Ezra’s commands to Jewish men to divorce their heathen wives ({{Ezra 9|Ezra 9-10}}).

*Text-critical note:* The verb שָׂנֵא (saneʾ) appears to be a third person form, “he hates,” which makes little sense in the context, unless one emends the following word to a third person verb as well. Then one might translate, “he [who] hates [his wife] [and] divorces her…is guilty of violence.” A similar translation is advocated by M. A. Shields, “Syncretism and Divorce in Malachi 2, 10-16, ” *ZAW* 111 (1999): 81-85. However, it is possible that the first person pronoun אָנֹכִי (ʾanokhi, “I”) has accidentally dropped from the text after כִּי (ki). If one restores the pronoun, the form שָׂנֵא can be taken as a participle and the text translated, “for I hate” (so NAB, NASB, NRSV, NLT).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “him who covers his garment with violence” (similar ASV, NRSV). Here “garment” is a metaphor for appearance and “violence” a metonymy of effect for cause. God views divorce as an act of violence against the victim.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the eyes of the Lord.”

*Translator's note:* In Hebrew the phrase “my messenger” is מַלְאָכִי (malʾakhi), the same form as the prophet’s name (see note on the name “Malachi” in {{Malachi 1:1|1:1}}). However, here the messenger appears to be an eschatological figure who is about to appear, as the following context suggests. According to {{Malachi 4:5|4:5}}, this messenger is “Elijah the prophet,” whom the NT identifies as John the Baptist ({{Matthew 11:10|Matt 11:10}}; {{Mark 1:2|Mark 1:2}}) because he came in the “spirit and power” of Elijah ({{Matthew 11:14|Matt 11:14}}; {{Matthew 17:11|17:11-12}}; Lk 1:17).

*Translator's note:* Here the Hebrew term הָאָדוֹן (haʾadon) is used, not יְהוָה (yehvah, typically rendered Lord). Thus the focus is not on the Lord as the covenant God, but on his role as master.

*Study note:* This *messenger of the covenant* may be equated with *my messenger* (that is, Elijah) mentioned earlier in the verse, or with *the Lord* himself. In either case the messenger functions as an enforcer of the covenant. Note the following verses, which depict purifying judgment on a people that has violated the Lord’s covenant.
*Study note:* The *refiner’s fire* was used to purify metal and refine it by melting it and allowing the dross, which floated to the top, to be scooped off.

*Translator's note:* The first person pronoun (a reference to the Lord) indicates that the Lord himself now speaks (see also v. {{Malachi 3:1|1}}). The prophet speaks in vv. {{Malachi 3:2|2-4}} (see also {{Malachi 2:17|2:17}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “those who swear [oaths] falsely.” Cf. NIV “perjurers”; TEV “those who give false testimony”; NLT “liars.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and against the oppressors of the worker for a wage, [the] widow and orphan.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “those who turn aside.”

*Study note:* Cf. {{Exodus 22:21|Exod 22:21}}; Lev 19:33-34; {{Deuteronomy 10:18|Deut 10:18-19}}; {{Deuteronomy 24:14|24:14}}, {{Deuteronomy 24:17|17}}; {{Deuteronomy 27:19|27:19}}; Jer 22:3; Zech 7:10.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “do not change.” This refers to God’s ongoing commitment to his covenant promises to Israel.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “turned aside from.”

*Translator's note:* Or “statutes” (so NAB, NASB, NRSV); NIV “decrees”; NLT “laws.”

*Text-critical note:* The LXX presupposes an underlying Hebrew text of עָקַב (ʿaqav, “deceive”), a metathesis of קָבַע (qavaʿ, “rob”), in all four uses of the verb here (vv. {{Malachi 3:8|8-9}}). The intent probably is to soften the impact of “robbing” God, but the language of the passage is intentionally bold and there is no reason to go against the reading of the MT (which is followed here by most English versions).

*Study note:* The *tithes and contributions* mentioned here are probably those used to sustain the Levites (see {{Numbers 18:8|Num 18:8}}, {{Numbers 18:11|11}}, {{Numbers 18:19|19}}, {{Numbers 18:21|21-24}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “cursed with a curse” that is, “under a curse” (so NIV, NLT, CEV).

*Translator's note:* The phrase “is guilty” is not present in the Hebrew text but is implied, and has been supplied in the translation for clarification and stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew phrase בֵּית הָאוֹצָר (bet haʾotsar, here translated “storehouse”) refers to a kind of temple warehouse described more fully in Nehemiah (where the term לִשְׁכָּה גְדוֹלָה [lishkah gedolah, “great chamber”] is used) as a place for storing grain, frankincense, temple vessels, wine, and oil (Neh 13:5). Cf. TEV “to the Temple.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the eater” (אֹכֵל, ʾokhel), a general term for any kind of threat to crops and livelihood. This is understood as a reference to a locust plague by a number of English versions: NAB, NRSV “the locust”; NIV “pests”; NCV, TEV “insects.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and I will rebuke for you the eater and it will not ruin for you the fruit of the ground.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will be” (so NAB, NRSV); TEV “your land will be a good place to live in.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your words are hard [or “strong”] against me”; cf. NIV84 “said harsh things against me”; NIV11 “spoken arrogantly against me”; TEV, NLT “said terrible things about me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “What [is the] profit”; NIV11 “What do we gain.”

*Study note:* The people’s public display of self-effacing piety has gone unrewarded by the Lord. The reason, of course, is that it was blatantly hypocritical.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “built up” (so NASB); NIV, NRSV “prosper”; NLT “get rich.”

*Translator's note:* Or “test”; NRSV, CEV “put God to the test.”

*Translator's note:* Or “fear” (so NAB); NRSV “revered”; NCV “honored.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “heard and listened”; NAB “listened attentively.”

*Study note:* The *scroll* mentioned here is a “memory book” (סֵפֶר זִכָּרוֹן, sefer zikkaron) in which the Lord keeps an ongoing record of the names of all the redeemed (see {{Exodus 32:32|Exod 32:32}}; {{Isaiah 4:3|Isa 4:3}}; Dan 12:1; Rev 20:12-15).

*Study note:* The Hebrew word סְגֻלָּה (segullah, “special property”) is a technical term referring to all the recipients of God’s redemptive grace, especially Israel ({{Exodus 19:5|Exod 19:5}}; {{Deuteronomy 7:6|Deut 7:6}}; {{Deuteronomy 14:2|14:2}}; {{Deuteronomy 26:18|26:18}}). The Lord says here that he will not forget even one individual in the day of judgment and reward.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you will see between.” Cf. NRSV, TEV, NLT “see the difference.”

*Study note:* Beginning with 4:1, the verse numbers through 4:6 in the English Bible differ from the verse numbers in the Hebrew text (*BHS*), with 4:1 ET = 3:19 HT, 4:2 ET = 3:20 HT, etc., through 4:6 ET = 3:24 HT. Thus the book of Malachi in the Hebrew Bible has only three chapters, with 24 verses in ch. 3.

*Study note:* This *day* is the well-known “day of the Lord” so pervasive in OT eschatological texts (see Joel 2:30-31; {{Amos 5:18|Amos 5:18}}; {{Obadiah 15|Obad 15}}). For the believer it is a day of grace and salvation; for the sinner, a day of judgment and destruction.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “so that it” (so NASB, NRSV). For stylistic reasons a new sentence was begun here in the translation.

*Study note:* The expression *the sun of vindication will rise* is a metaphorical way of describing the day of the Lord as a time of restoration when God vindicates his people (see {{2 Samuel 23:4|2 Sam 23:4}}; {{Isaiah 30:26|Isa 30:26}}; {{Isaiah 60:1|60:1}}, {{Isaiah 60:3|3}}). Their vindication and restoration will be as obvious and undeniable as the bright light of the rising sun.

*Translator's note:* Here the Hebrew word צְדָקָה (tsedaqah), usually translated “righteousness” (so KJV, NIV, NRSV, NLT; cf. NAB “justice”), has been rendered as “vindication” because it is the vindication of God’s people that is in view in the context. Cf. BDB 842 s.v. צְדָקָה 6; “*righteousness* as vindicated, *justification*, *salvation*, etc.”

*Study note:* The point of the metaphor of *healing wings* is unclear. The sun seems to be compared to a bird. Perhaps the sun’s “wings” are its warm rays. “Healing” may refer to a reversal of the injury done by evildoers (see {{Malachi 3:5|Mal 3:5}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you will go out and skip about.”

*Study note:* *Horeb* is another name for Mount Sinai (cf. {{Exodus 3:1|Exod 3:1}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “which I commanded him in Horeb concerning all Israel, statutes and ordinances.”

*Study note:* *I will send you Elijah the prophet*. In light of the ascension of Elijah to heaven without dying ({{2 Kings 2:11|2 Kgs 2:11}}), Judaism has always awaited his return as an aspect of the messianic age (see, e.g., {{John 1:19|John 1:19-28}}). Jesus identified John the Baptist as Elijah because he came in the “spirit and power” of his prototype Elijah ({{Matthew 11:14|Matt 11:14}}; {{Matthew 17:1|17:1-13}}; {{Mark 9:2|Mark 9:2-13}}; Luke 9:28-36).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he will turn the heart[s] of [the] fathers to [the] sons, and the heart[s] of [the] sons to their fathers.” This may mean that the messenger will encourage reconciliation of conflicts within Jewish families in the postexilic community (see {{Malachi 2:10|Mal 2:10}}; this interpretation is followed by most English versions). Another option is to translate, “he will turn the hearts of the fathers together with those of the children [to me], and the hearts of the children together with those of their fathers [to me].” In this case the prophet encourages both the younger and older generations of sinful society to repent and return to the Lord (cf. {{Malachi 3:7|Mal 3:7}}). This option is preferred in the present translation; see Beth Glazier-McDonald, *Malachi* (SBLDS), 256.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[the] ban” (חֵרֶם, kherem). God’s prophetic messenger seeks to bring about salvation and restoration, thus avoiding the imposition of the covenant curse, that is, the divine ban that the hopelessly unrepentant must expect (see {{Deuteronomy 7:2|Deut 7:2}}; {{Deuteronomy 20:17|20:17}}; {{Judges 1:21|Judg 1:21}}; Zech 14:11). If the wicked repent, the purifying judgment threatened in {{Malachi 4:1|4:1-3}} will be unnecessary.
